runs.text: da que ſe propoem, ou arrezoar ſobre ella.

lines.note: Continues a definition from the preceding page: the question being proposed, or reasoning about it. The opening da is only the surviving continuation, not a new entry.

Mondoo is question and answer or disputation, paraphrased by toi, kotayuru. The divided Mon- starts the example continued on the next row; the headword begins at the column margin, not at continuation indentation.
Mon-doo ni oyobu means entering into a disputation. Saiuǒno begins the quoted expression about a further round of discussion.

The quotation prohibits renewing the disputation. Taif. is the source label, followed by Lib. for its book number. Its final letter has a broken upper hook; Taif. is retained rather than confidently changing the damaged type to t.

runs.text: 28. Não ha pera que replicar, ou ſegundar a-

lines.note: Book 28 is followed by the Portuguese explanation: there is no need to reply or repeat the dispute. The printed a- is retained even though the article and following noun remain separate words in interpretation.
Completes the preceding translation, then gives mondoo suru as another way to say dispute. The paragraph sign separates the example, not a new physical row.
Moonen is explained as disorderly thoughts, midarina nen, and glossed as evil thoughts. The caron is visible and is not replaced from modern vowel expectations.

The imperative setdan seyo tells the reader to cut off the bad thoughts. The second Japanese expression is retained as printed mǒriuo rather than silently replacing it with an expected doctrinal compound; Cortai begins its translation.
Completes Cortai pellos maos pensamentos, cutting through or putting an end to evil thoughts. This is the translation of the imperative above, not a separate sense.
Mongatame denotes the duty of guarding and defending the gate. The scan shows the doubled f in Officio and the f of defen-, not a long s.
Completes defender a porta, then names the people who perform gate duty, mongatame no shuu. Os begins their Portuguese description.
The people mentioned above are those who hold this office. The middle of tem is lightly printed; its reading follows the remaining strokes and the relative clause.

runs.text: Mongiacu. Momi tçuqu. i, Monouo iro-

lines.note: Monjaku is paraphrased by rubbing or repeatedly handling an object. The synonym is read tçuqu from the scan, retaining the historical q spelling; iro- continues as iroironi below.
Iroironi toriatsukoo describes handling something in various ways. The Portuguese likewise begins moving and handling it; the tilde in tratã- is retained rather than expanded.

runs.text: do muito com as mãos algũa couſa. ¶

lines.note: Completes the description of much handling with the hands. Miuo starts the bodily example, with the object particle attached to mi in the printed spelling.
Mi wo monjaku suru means moving or rubbing the body. Bulir and esfregar correct the OCR's Butir and esfiegar; the short s before f is retained.

Monjuu is paraphrased as kado no uchi, within the gate. The supplied NINJAL index (165c05) prompted reinspection: the final character is a damaged marked u, not n. The caron reading remains slightly uncertain because one arm is weak; the social extension follows below.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Dentro dalgũa familia, ou ſeita,

lines.note: The second sense is being within a household or religious group. Familia and seita describe the social extension of the gate image.

runs.text: ou entre os dalgũa familia, ou ſeita.

lines.note: Completes the social sense as being among the members of a household or sect. The scan supports familia, not the OCR's famitia.

runs.text: Mongiǔxo. Toi, xiruſu tocoro. i, Cujino

lines.note: Monjuusho denotes a place for inquiries and records, further explained through adjudication or litigation. The damaged headword vowel is read o, not OCR e; Cujino continues into the following row.
Kujino satadokoro completes the Japanese explanation of a hearing or judicial office. The Portuguese describes a house or place of audience, without asserting a modern institutional equivalent.
Mongon is the wording of a written document or letter. The Portuguese gloss concerns its phrasing and style; eſ- continues into estilo below.
Completes the letter-style gloss and contrasts good wording with iyashii wording. The printed l introduces the alternative, while iya- remains divided at the row boundary.

runs.text: Ser o eſtilo da carta bom, ou mao.

lines.note: Completes iyashii, here opposed to good style. The Portuguese explicitly interprets the contrast as a letter's style being good or bad.
Mongwai is explained by kado no hoka, outside the gate. The spelling guai is preserved rather than reduced to a modern unrounded syllable.
Portal completes the preceding alternative for the entrance or gateway. The short continuation remains its own physical line.
Monguchi denotes the gate entrance. The scan supports the ch sequence and the full Portuguese porta, correcting Mongueni and prta in the draft.
Monja is a questioner, explained as one who asks. The mark over o in Tò is visibly a single grave-shaped stroke here; it is retained rather than regularized to a circumflex.
Completes the definition of a questioner as someone who raises a doubt or question. The tilde in algũa is retained on u.

runs.text: Peça da China, ou veo delgado de ſe-

lines.note: This separate monja entry names a thin Chinese silk fabric, not a questioner. The damaged last headword letter is read a from its remaining right side and the textile context; ſe- continues as seda.

Completes the fabric description: silk described as raw and patterned. The scan clearly retains iſa where liſa would be expected; no distinct initial l can be recovered, so it is not silently supplied. This damaged or defective word remains a nonblocking caveat.
Monzen is kado no mae, in front of the gate. It begins a spatial entry distinct from the identically spelled book title below.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Caſas que eſtão fora da porta da

lines.note: The extended sense names houses outside a temple gate. Te- begins the Japanese word Tera embedded in the Portuguese explanation; its upright type is retained across the division.
Ra completes Tera, immediately glossed as a monastery. Monzen ni ichi wo na- begins the expression about making a marketplace or crowd at the gate.

runs.text: Ajuntarſe muita gente a porta, & fa-

lines.note: Na-su completes the Japanese example. Its Portuguese interpretation describes many people gathering at the gate, with fa- continuing into fazer below.
Completes fazer aparato e estrondo: creating a conspicuous display and commotion. The low-s st construction is retained without a global ligature normalization.
This Monjen is a Chinese book title, separate from the preceding gate expression. The unusual printed liruo is retained rather than silently reordered to liuro; the preposition reads da, not OCR du.

runs.text: Dignidade alta entre os Bõzos, que

lines.note: Monzeki is described as a high Buddhist clerical rank. The explanation continues with the kinds of families from which its holders usually come.

runs.text: ordinariamente anda em filhos, ou parentes

lines.note: The rank is ordinarily held by sons or relatives of the person named on the next row. The visible line starts at continuation indentation, which the provisional layout had omitted.

runs.text: chegados do Rey, ou em Cungues nobres.

lines.note: Completes the account with close royal relatives or noble kuge. Cungues is the embedded Japanese rank-name in Portuguese plural form; its local italic printing is retained.
Monzet is fainting or loss of consciousness, paraphrased by modae and tayuru. The scan supports Monjet and final tayuru, correcting the OCR's extra m and final a; alie- continues into alienação.

Completes alienation of the senses, then introduces a compound expression for collapsing or fainting. The short mark in Mõjet is provisionally treated as an abbreviation tilde replacing n, not as a long-o caron; its small impression remains uncertain.

runs.text: car deſmayado, ou fora de ſi.

lines.note: Fi-car completes the translation: becoming faint or losing awareness of oneself. The short continuation finishes the preceding compound example.
Monji denotes written characters of China or Japan. The Portuguese country-name spelling and tilde are preserved as printed.
Monjin first means asking or raising a question. The abbreviated Itẽ introduces a different, common usage developed across the column break.

runs.text: Ficar concluido, ou conuencido ſem falar. Eſ-

lines.note: The further meaning is being silenced by an argument or conceding defeat. The final word begins Eſ-, not the OCR's Et-; its continuation is on the next row.

runs.text: te he oſentido, que ordinariamente corre.

lines.note: Completes Este and states that this is the usual meaning. The damaged interior of oſentido is retained in the printed close spacing, while the final corre has two r types.

Continues the preceding column's common sense of monjin: I acknowledge myself defeated or convinced. The scan gives Monjinſuru without the OCR's extra i, and Doume por conuencido rather than its garbled Portuguese.

runs.text: Eſcritura, ou papel eſcrito, que fica

lines.note: Monjo is a written record or document that is kept. This independent entry begins at the margin, not at continuation indentation.

runs.text: pera o diante, ou tempo futuro.

lines.note: The written record remains for later or future times. This completes the archival sense of monjo rather than adding a separate object.

runs.text: Monin. l, mǒmocunin. i, Me xijta fito.

lines.note: Monin and moomokunin denote a blind person, paraphrased by me shiita hito. The first headword vowel is weakly printed; no accent is supplied there solely from the clearly marked alternative.
The single Portuguese word identifies the preceding pair as blind. Its brevity does not make this a heading or page furniture.
Monmoo is inability to read or write. The example begins with an abbreviated Mõ-, whose short tilde represents the n before the next row's mǒna rather than a second long-o mark.

runs.text: Homem que não ſabe ler, nem

lines.note: Together with Mõ- above, mǒna fito describes an illiterate person. The Portuguese says he cannot read or write; the worn middle letter of nem is read as e rather than the OCR's i.
Completes the inability-to-write clause. The continuation is kept as its own physical line.
Monmon kuku denotes words and clauses of a written text. The headword ends in n, not the OCR's m; eſ- starts escritura below.
The example concerns attending to each phrase of a text. Monmõ abbreviates the final n of monmon with a visible tilde; to- begins tomuru on the following line.
Tomuru completes kokoro wo tomuru, paying attention. The Portuguese paraphrases stopping to consider each word, divided as pala-ura here.
Completes palavra and adds each written sentence or clause. The scan supports ſentença, not the OCR's ſemença.
Monnan means posing difficult questions, paraphrased by katai koto wo too. The baseline punctuation before i is retained rather than adding a headword stop that is not securely visible.
Completes the explanation as asking difficult or doubtful things. Mon- begins the example monnan wo kakuru below.
Monnan wo kakuru is putting difficult questions or objections. The damaged Portuguese word is read difficultoſas from its surviving types, not normalized from the OCR's dificaltoſas.
Completes the definition by specifying argument about those difficult questions. This is continuous Portuguese explanatory text, not a new example.

runs.text: Couſa. Ante posta eſta palaura à raiz de

lines.note: Mono first means a thing. The grammatical explanation begins by describing its placement before a verb stem; Ante corrects OCR Aute without modernizing the printed two-word spacing.
Prefixed mono can designate a person habitually engaged in an activity. The worn verbos and peßoa are recoverable from the remaining print and the grammatical sentence.

runs.text: deſtra no que ſignifica o verbo. Vt,

lines.note: The person is practiced or skilled in what the verb denotes. Mo- begins the example monokaki; the damaged letters in deſtra and ſignifica are read with the complete construction.
Monokaki is a writer or scribe, while monoii is a speaker or talker. These are examples of the preceding prefix construction rather than independent headwords in the margin.

runs.text: ¶ Postpondoſe ſignifica a couſa que recebe a

lines.note: The explanation now turns to mono after a verb stem, denoting the thing that receives the action. The printed Postpondoſe spelling is retained.
Completes the explanation of the affected object and gives agemono as an offering. Of- continues into offerta on the next physical line.
After completing the offering gloss, kuimono illustrates food and Faqi- begins the footwear example. Each paragraph sign separates an example within the same entry.
Faqimono is footwear. The entry then gives mono wo miru an idiomatic sense involving a horse shying; the abbreviated Portuguese Eſpã- continues below.

runs.text: tarſe o caualo de ſubito quãdo vai caminhando.

lines.note: Completes the explanation of a horse suddenly taking fright while walking. Caminhando is continuous in the print, not the OCR's ca minhando; the tilde abbreviation in quãdo remains unexpanded.
Mono wo miru uma describes a horse prone to shying. The Portuguese adjective is divided at the row boundary.
Completes espantadiço, easily startled. This short row closes the horse example and the first Mono entry.
A separate Mono entry gives the personal meaning, a person. It is not a continuation of the preceding noun meaning thing.

Monobukai describes a weighty or composed person who appears to possess knowledge and judgment. Enlargement of the worn Portuguese noun supports the broken double-s ligature Peßoa rather than OCR Pejoa; the detached upper stroke is not treated as an accent.
Completes the description with great knowledge and judgment. The spelling juizo is preserved without adding a modern accent.
Monobukasa is the nominal form corresponding to monobukai, referring to that depth or gravity. Its isolated form is an indented derivative row, not an omitted Portuguese gloss.
Monobukoo supplies the corresponding adverbial form. The visible caron and separate derivative row are preserved.

runs.text: Couſa que não he de muito momen-

lines.note: Monokawa is explained as something of little importance. The gloss continues momento below rather than ending the entry at this row.

runs.text: to, ou he inferior comparada com outra.

lines.note: Completes the notion of little weight or something inferior by comparison with another. The scan supports comparada, correcting comperada in the draft.
Monokusai is glossed here as feeling indisposed or ill. The historical Portuguese indeſposto is preserved rather than standardized.
Monokusai nari describes the manner or condition of being thus unwell. The Japanese example and its Portuguese explanation continue into the next row.
Completes mal deſposto, being out of sorts. This is the close of the preceding example, not a separate lexical entry.

runs.text: Couſa que ſendo leue, ou de

lines.note: Monogamashii describes presenting a slight matter as weighty. The scan supports ſendo and de, replacing the OCR's senda and da.

runs.text: pouco momento ſe dà, ou mostra por couſa que

lines.note: The thing has little importance but is offered or displayed as though important. This explanatory continuation is visibly indented in the scan.
Completes the contrast with something that counts or matters. The final upright X. is the regional usage label, not part of the italic prose.
Monoganashii describes sadness or melancholy. The printed st form is preserved without attempting the separately deferred ligature audit.
Monoganashisa is the corresponding noun for sadness. The final damaged vowel has the a form, correcting the OCR's Monoganaxiſi.
Monoganashuu is the corresponding adverbial form. The compact long-u mark remains provisionally a caron, matching the supplied reading; its heavy impression is noted rather than silently recast.
Monogatari is conversation or discourse in this gloss. Monogatariuo begins the verbal example with its attached object particle.
Completes monogatari wo suru, conversing. The short continuation is indented in the scan, despite the draft's flush-left placement.
Monogonomi denotes curiosity or appetite for various things. The scan restores the missing t in apetite; va- continues into varias below.
Completes varias cousas and begins an alternative adjectival or personal use. The final Monogonomi has no t; the example continues onto f331, anticipated by the separate mono- catchword.

zones.label: Printed catchword

lines.note: The far-right catchword anticipates monogonomina at the start of f331. Its roman type and printed hyphen are retained; it is not a body line.
